related.en: family feast of the patron saint

note:
Besides the family Слава, there is also a Slava of a city or a school.

Cities:
• Belgrade - Спасовдан
• Novi Sad - Ђурђиц

This is not Дан града (City Day), so do not mix them up.

Schoolchildren have their own Slava - Са̀виндан, St Sava's Day, 27 January: no lessons, and the pupils put on concerts. Да̑н сту̀дена̄та̄ (Students' Day) is 4 April.
title: School and city Slava

note:
On 14 February people split into two camps: some celebrate St Trifun's Day (Трифундан), others Valentine's Day (Дан заљубљених).

Све̑тӣ Три̏фӯн is the patron saint of winemakers, and on this day the vines (ло̏за) are pruned.

Couples send each other rhymed text-message confessions.
title: Trifun or Valentine

related.en: little rascal, ringleader (said of a boy, jokingly)

note:
Serbs know how to call children tenderly: «зла̑то» (gold), «срце мамино» (mommy's heart), «мѝшӣћ» (little mouse), «бубица» (little bug), «лепо̀тица» (beauty), «слаткица» (sweetie), «шѐћер» (sugar), «паху̀љица» (snowflake), «мѐзимица» (darling), «шећерле̏ма» (sweet tooth).

A boy is jokingly called «харамба̀ша», and a spoiled child «мамина маза».
title: Pet names for children

note:
Годишња доба: про̀леће, ле̏то, је̏се̄н, зи́ма. A Serb lists the seasons starting with spring.

There are special adverbs for the past: ле̏то̄с, јесѐнас, зѝмӯс, про̀лето̄с (last summer, autumn, winter, spring).

Also:
• «михољско лето» - Indian summer
• «преступна година» - leap year

People jokingly speak of a «тринаеста плата» (a thirteenth salary) in state jobs.
title: The seasons in Serbian

related.en: a glass of rakija as a welcome

note:
A guest is welcomed with «ракија добродошлица» - a glass of rakija as a greeting.

To thank someone, you invite them «на кафу» (кафа захвалница) or to lunch. A gift can be chocolate, a bottle of alcohol, a souvenir or a present for the children.

On receiving a gift, Serbs open it at once in front of the giver and express surprise: «Јао, није требало…»
title: Rakija and coffee as thanks

note:
School in Serbia:
• a генера́ција (age cohort) runs from 1 March to 28 February: everyone born in that period starts school in the same year
• the year before school is a compulsory preparatory group (прѐдшколско)
• о̀сновна шко̑ла lasts 8 years (4+4)
• then срѐдња шко̑ла: a гѝмна̄зија for 4 years or a vocational school for 3
• pupils study for 12 years in all

Children first write in Cyrillic, then Latin is added. They write in pencil and there is no school diary. Serbs picture the week as a row of days, not a circle.
title: School in Serbia

related.en: house guardian (an egg kept for a year)

note:
In Serbia people do not bake Easter cakes, so they dye and bless eggs (фарбати јаја).

Customs:
• red eggs are a must on the table, and one of them is kept until the next Easter as a «чува̀ркућа»
• children play «туцање јајима» (egg tapping)
• the bunny (ускршњи зец) brings gifts in a basket: the day before, children gather grass for it

The greeting: «Христос васкрсе!» - «Ваистину васкрсе!».
title: Easter in Serbia

skip: false friends with Russian: only for Russian speakers

related.en: sour cherry, also a woman's name
a woman's name (felt to be Russian)
Petar Petrović, the Serbian counterpart of John Smith

note:
Suffixes:
• -ка does not make a name rude, on the contrary it is affectionate: Сашка, Машка, Мирка
• -ица gives a tender form: Машица, Ољица

Many women's names are berries and fruits: Ја̏года, Ви̏шња, Ма̀лина, Ду̏ња.

The Serbian counterpart of John Smith is Пѐтар Пѐтровић.

Ве̏ра, На́да, Љу́бав are Faith, Hope and Love.
title: Serbian names and diminutives

related.en: the first half of the day (before noon)

note:
Serbs divide the day roughly like this:
• ју̏тро̄с - morning, about 3-9 am
• препо́дне - before noon
• у по́дне - 12 noon
• попо́дне - after lunch until 3 pm
• послепо́дне - about 3-7 pm
• ве̏че̄ - 7-11 pm
• у по̏но̄ћ - midnight

The boundaries are loose.

For «tomorrow» the same words go with су̏тра: су̏тра у̀јутру, су̏тра попо́дне, су̏тра у̏вече̄.

Also: пре̏кјуче̄ - the day before yesterday, преко̀сутра - the day after tomorrow.
title: Times of day: rough boundaries

note:
Titles of Russian books are often translated into Serbian:
• «Ра̏т и ми̑р»
• «Зло̀чин и ка̏зна»
• «Ју̀на̄к на̏ше̄г до̑ба»
• «Мртве душе»
• «Тешко паметном»
• «Вишњик»
• «Галеб»
• «Дама са псетанцетом»
• «Зли̑ ду̏си»
• «Мајстор и Маргарита»

Surnames are spelled differently: Достојевски, Гогољ, Љермонтов.
title: Russian classics in Serbian

note:
Eateries are named after the main dish plus the suffix -ница or -џиница, which marks a place:
• ћевабџѝница - ћевапи
• бурегџѝница - burek
• палачѝнкарница - pancakes
• посластѝчарница - pastry shop
title: Eateries ending in -ница

related.en: tongue twister: On top of the hill the willow sways

note:
In Serbian the letter «р» can be a vowel sound, so a word can do without vowels: вр̏т, пр̏ст, кр̑в, смр̏т, кр̏ст, бр̑з, ср̏це, цр̑ква, Ср̀бија.

The sound can be drawn out, like a growl.

For practice there is a tongue twister: «На врх брда врба мрда».
title: Syllabic R: words almost without vowels

skip: about Russian names and Russian-language paperwork in Serbia

note:
Serbian names many things after peoples and cities, and not always the way English does:
• јапа̀нке - flip-flops
• фра̀нцӯскӣ крѐвет - a double bed
• амѐричкӣ пла̀кар - a built-in wardrobe
• шве̏дскӣ сто̑ - a buffet
• руска салата - Russian salad (Olivier)
• ру̏скӣ ча̏ј - black tea
• па̀ризер - a boiled sausage like bologna
• венецијанери - blinds
• шпанска села - something incomprehensible (literally «Spanish villages»)
title: Countries and cities in the names of things

note:
Serbian sounds:
• клај-клај - choo-choo (a train)
• куц-куц - knock-knock
• пу-пу-пу - touch wood (said with a knock)
• фу̏ј, бља̏к - yuck
• пих - what a stink
• пст - shh
• ауч - ouch
• ср̑к - slurp
• хрк - snore
• хик - hiccup
• цмок - smooch
• ју̀пи - yippee

Animals are called and chased away with different words:
• мац-мац - to call a cat
• чи̏бе - to chase a dog
• ши̏ц - to chase a cat

Ма̏ јо̏к means «of course not», но но means «tut-tut». After a sneeze people say «На̀здравље».
title: Interjections and sound words

note:
Words for a corner and a dead end:
• ћо̀шак - a corner, from Turkish, colloquial
• со̀ка̄к - a lane; today found in songs or used ironically
• ћорсо̀ка̄к - a dead end; in everyday speech it is replaced by the calque слепа улица
• ку́так - a cozy nook, a rare word

The neutral word for a corner is у̏гао.
title: Turkisms: ћошак, сокак, ћорсокак

note:
Colors that surprise:
• пла̑ва - blue, light blue and blond at once: пла̑ва ко̀са, пла̀вуша
• црвена коса - red (ginger) hair
• црно вино - red wine (literally «black wine»)
• модра - dark blue, мо̏дрица - a bruise
• тѐгет - a dark navy that is almost black
• смеђа and бра̏он - brown; смеђе очи - brown eyes
• жута минута - a momentary lapse (literally «a yellow minute»)
title: Colors that surprise

note:
Many neutral Serbian words are made of two roots:
• главо̀боља - head + pain
• зубо̀боља, врто̀главица
• пољопрѝвреда - field + farming
• мравојед, пуно̀главац
• чува̀ркућа - houseleek

Some words are emotionally colored: пу̏столо̄в, сладоку́сац, да̏нгуба, вѐтропир, цепѝдлака, про̀бисвет, џа̀балебарош, ра̀спикућа, брзо̀плет, тврдо̀глав.
title: Funny compound words

related.en: the second evening of New Year, 1 January
family feast of the patron saint

note:
New Year in Serbia is more modest than Christmas and Slava.

How it is celebrated:
1. It starts in the daytime on 31 December: people book a table at a bar in advance, there may be an entrance fee, and live music plays (дневна журка).
2. By evening many go home to rest.
3. The evening of 1 January is called реприза Нове године.

Gifts go mostly to children.
title: New Year in Serbia: the daytime party

note:
Five working words for everyday talk:
• Може - agreeing to an offer: «Може ли ракија?» - «Може!»
• Ва̏жи - «all right, deal» in reply to a suggestion
• Хо̀ћу - «I'll do it», a stand-alone answer to a request
• Ни̏шта (ма̏ ни̏шта) - the answer to an apology or thanks
• Гу̑жва - traffic jams and crowds; «У гу̑жвӣ сам» explains both forgetfulness and being busy
title: Five working words for everyday talk

note:
In Serbian society men are praised not only for what they do but also for how they look: you may hear «ле̑п ка̏о лу̏тка» (pretty as a doll).

«Good-looking» to a Serb means neat, well groomed, tall, not heavy.

Praise for character:
• сна́жан, духо̀вит, бри̏жан, о̏дгово̄ран
• по̀штен, хра́бар, о̏длӯчан, у̏по̄ран
title: Compliments to men in Serbian

related.en: a town whose whole name fits on a plate

note:
Serbian license plates carry two letters, the city code:
• BG - Београд
• NS - Нови Сад
• NI - Ниш
• KG - Крагујевац
• SU - Суботица

RU is Рума, not Russia. Only the town of Уб has its whole name on the plate (UB).

Montenegro also uses city codes: PG - Подгорица, BD - Будва. Bosnia has had no city codes since 1998, only letters that are written the same in both alphabets.
title: Letters on Serbian license plates

note:
Serbian has about 8000 active Turkisms:
• ча̀рапа, ко̀мшија, џе̏п, ду̀гме
• ја̀стук, то́рба, буда̀ла, џа̏бе̄

From German came бѝна, ки́фла, фле̏ка, ци́гла, шпо̏рет, штѝкла, шра̀фцӣгер.

From Italian: пѝјаца, ру́жа, о̏пера. From Hungarian: гу̏ла̄ш, со̏ба, чи̏зме.

A henpecked husband is called папу̀чар, from па̀пуча (slipper).
title: Serbian and other languages

note:
Many Serbian words are adjectives that became nouns:
• запо̏сленӣ - employee
• надре̏ђенӣ - superior
• подређени, дежу̏рнӣ, осу̏мњиченӣ, ухапшени

Short everyday names arose the same way: до̀ма̄ћӣ (homework), во̀зачка (driver's license), хитна (ambulance), да̀љӣнскӣ (remote control), ку̀па̄ћӣ (swimsuit).

They decline like adjectives: о новом запосленом.
title: Adjectives used as nouns

skip: about Russian products missing in Serbia: written for Russian expats

note:
Serbian renders foreign names by sound:
• Конфучије, Бу́да, Питагора, Микеланђело
• Џорџ Вашингтон, Виктор Иго, Алберт Ајнштајн, Ле Корбизије
• Јованка Орлеанка (Joan of Arc), Па̑па Фра̏ња (Pope Francis), Луј (Louis)

Rulers are named like this: Пѐтар Вѐликӣ (Peter the Great), Катарина Велика (Catherine the Great).
title: Names of famous people in Serbian

note:
In Serbia many characters go by their own names:
• Bugs Bunny - Душко Дугоушко
• Donald Duck - Паја Патак
• Goofy - Шиља
• Scrooge McDuck - Ба́ја Па́так
• Woody Woodpecker - Пера Детлић
• Tinker Bell - Звончица
• Captain Hook - Ку̏ка

Others stayed as they are: Том и Џери, Петар Пан, Шре̏к.

A bogeyman or monster in Serbian is ба̀ук.
title: Cartoon characters, Serbian style

note:
You can call a Serb a ко̏њ, ма̀гарац or ма̀јмун, but not a goat: ја̏рац is Capricorn from the horoscope, and the Serb will simply think you mean his sign.

People use the vocative: Коњу! Магарче! Ма̀јмуне! The last one is considered very insulting.

You can make it stronger: Коњу један!
title: Animal insults

note:
Serbian has words that exist only in the plural:
• neuter: вра́та, ле́ђа, ко̏ла
• гру̑ди, дѐснӣ, на̏оча̄ре, пантало́не
• фа̀рмерке, га̏ће, но̀вине, ме̏рдевине
• feminine: гра̀буље

They agree as plurals: ова врата су дрвена, у овим фармеркама, ићи колима.
title: Words that exist only in the plural

related.en: utilities: water, central heating, garbage collection, stairwell cleaning

note:
On the bills look for:
• рачун за струју, грѐја̄ње, во̀да, и̏нтернет
• и̏нфостан - utilities: water, central heating, garbage collection, stairwell cleaning

Electricity is split into вишу тарифу (daytime, ску̏па стру́ја) and нижу (nighttime, јѐфтина стру́ја).

Further down the bill:
• бро̀јило, потро̀шња
• у̀купно за пла́ћа̄ње, ро̏к за пла́ћа̄ње
• ка̏мата - late fee
title: Utility bills

skip: about Russian patronymics, which English speakers do not have either

related.en: I know it from A to Z

note:
Besides Cyrillic (ћирѝлица) and Latin (латѝница), people in messages write «bald» Latin - ћелавица:
• no marks: c instead of č and ć, s instead of š, z instead of ž
• dj instead of đ

This causes mistakes: cackalica is чачка̀лица (toothpick), kuce is ку̏че (puppy) or ку̏ћа (house) depending on the context.

The alphabet has 30 letters, from «А» to «Ш»: «знам од А до Ш».
title: Ћелавица: informal Latin spelling

note:
Serbs depend a lot on the weather: in bad weather it is easy to cancel a meeting, but on a sunny weekend you cannot get into a restaurant without a booking, especially on an open terrace.

Call in the morning of the same day.

When the table is booked, you hear «Резервисано је!» Before eating: «При̏ја̄тно!»
title: Restaurants and the weather

note:
At a Serbian wedding a live band (жи̏ва сви̑рка) sets the mood.

The usual order:
1. world hits
2. Yugoslav rock (југорок)
3. popular folk songs
4. modern hits
5. ту̀рбофолк for the dance floor, and севдалинке

Towards morning the repertoire gets less picky. The hosts' task is to please the guests with food and music.
title: The music code of a Serbian wedding

related.en: volleyball player; Vanja is the name he is known by
short for Svetislav (also a male name)

note:
In Serbia an athlete may be written with two names: Владимир Вања Грбић, where Ва̏ња is the name he is known by.

Unexpected names:
• Страхиња - male
• Љу́ба - short for Љу̏бомӣр
• Света - from Све̏тислав, also male
• Ва̏ња is more often female

Other common names: Мима, Немања, Не̏на̄д, Бо̀јан.
title: Names and nicknames

note:
Пара̀дајз турѝзам is the ironic name for a kind of holiday where food is brought from home to the beach: canned goods, vegetables, sausage, tomatoes. The term appeared in the early 1980s, when holidays in Greece became popular.

Serbs spend the whole day on the beach: they arrive around ten and leave last. They complain about the heat («на̏пољу је па̀као») but do not hide from the sun.
title: Tomato tourism

related.sr: Са̏мо не̑к је жи̑во и здра̏во.
related.en: As long as it's alive and well.

note:
The word чо̏век means both «person» and «man», so for a woman people say о̏соба: она је оптимистична особа.

Forms of address for children: to a son - си̑не, to a daughter - ће̏ро, but a daughter is often addressed as си̑не too.

What people say about a newborn:
• a boy - «Прво, па мушко!»
• a girl - «Само нек је живо и здраво.»

In invitations the woman's name is written first.
title: Човек - a person and a man

note:
Ко̀шава is a strong, gusty south-east wind. It often blows in Belgrade and northern Serbia, most of all in autumn and winter.

It brings clear, cold weather and raises dust and snow. People complain about it as a weather phenomenon linked with headaches and tiredness.
title: The košava wind

note:
Serbian habits:
• they see no difference between tiger and leopard patterns - it is all «тиграсто»
• they love tracksuits
• they praise everything with the word ле̑по (nice, good, tasty)
• they peel cucumbers
• they do not like taking their shoes off
• at the first sign of a cold, the first thing is chamomile tea
• boiled milk is covered with a plate

They fear a draft (про̏маја), and «со̑к» also covers fizzy drinks.
title: Serbian habits

related.en: to register at the employment office

note:
Familiar ones: по̏шта, полѝција, бо́лница, шко̑ла, вр̀тић, су̑д.

Special ones:
• о̏пштина - the municipality, also the registry office
• месна заједница - the local community council
• ску̏пштина - parliament or a city assembly
• би̏ро - the employment office: прија́вити се на би̏ро
• со̏ција̄лно - social welfare; РФЗО - the health insurance fund
• за́вод - an institution

Public utilities: Градска чистоћа (garbage collection), Градско зеленило (parks), Путеви Србије (roads).
title: Institutions in Serbia

related.sr: Не̏ка ти се све̏ жѐље испу̀не!
related.en: May all your wishes come true!

note:
Serbs do not make long toasts: just «Жѝвели!»

Celebrations are more modest, without long feasts:
• cake and coffee on the table, snacks, often grilled meat
• bringing flowers is not customary

Congratulations are short: «Сре̏ћан ро̏ђенда̄н!», «Све̏ на̑јбоље!», «Нека ти се све жеље испуне!»

The 18th and 50th birthdays get special attention, and when a baby is born the father treats his friends.
title: A Serbian birthday

related.en: nickname for a woman from Vojvodina
nickname for a man from Vojvodina

note:
These came from Hungarian:
• бу̑нда, ва́рош, ва́шар, кѐцеља
• ло́пов, ма̏чка, пу́нђа, са̏ла̄ш
• со̏ба, ци̏пеле, чо̏по̄р, чи̏зме

Many Hungarians live in Vojvodina, and in 30 municipalities Hungarian is an official language.

Women of Vojvodina are jokingly called соса, men - ла̏ла.
title: Hungarian words in Serbian

related.en: summer version of ајвар with eggplant and tomatoes
a biscuit that no childhood is without

note:
Unfamiliar to a newcomer:
• а̀јва̄р and its summer version пѝнђур
• ки̏селӣ ку̀пус, кисело млеко, про̀ја, ка̀јмак
• чва̏рци, пр̏шута
• плазма - a biscuit that no childhood is without

Зе̏ље is sorrel or spinach, коре за питу are pastry sheets for pie.
title: What people eat in Serbia

skip: false friends with Russian: only for Russian speakers

note:
The numbers used to have two digits: police 92, fire brigade 93, ambulance 94. Now they are preceded by 1:
• полѝција - 192
• ватрогасци - 193
• хитна помоћ - 194

From a landline you could also dial 95: a machine announced the exact time, and an operator could wake you up on request. This is what the song «Окрени број 95» by the band Tap 011 is about.
title: Emergency numbers: 192, 193, 194

related.en: and that's the end of the story

note:
Serbs love rhyming doublings:
• ти̑п-то̏п (all great), туто комплето (all together), цикцак (zigzag)
• ђа̑к пр̀ва̄к (first-grader), касица-прасица (piggy bank)
• хокус-покус, ћирибу-ћириба - a magician's spell
• еци-пеци-пец - a counting-out rhyme
• икс-окс, крѝжић-кру́жић - tic-tac-toe
• рус-купус, муж-пуж - just for the rhyme

A fairy tale ends with «чича Мича, готова прича».
title: Rhyming pairs in Serbian

note:
These names are the same as Serbian words: Ду̏ња (quince), Ла̏ла (tulip), Лу́ка (port), На́на (mint), Вла́да (government), Сла̏ва (fame), Ри́ма (rhyme), Со̀фа (sofa), Ка̀мила (camel), Паша (pasture), Фо̏ка (seal), Ми̏ла (dear).

The names themselves are not translated, but they may make a Serb smile.
title: Names that are also Serbian words

note:
In Serbia a сла̏ва belongs not only to a family but also to a city, a church, a school, a trade and a company. Do not confuse it with City Day (Дан града).

Belgrade:
• Slava - Спасовдан (the 40th day after Easter)
• City Days - 16-19 April
• 20 October - Liberation Day

Novi Sad:
• Slava - Ђурђиц, 16 November
• City Day - 1 February

The school Slava is Савиндан, 27 January.
title: City Slava and City Day

related.en: Repetition is the mother of learning.
Mom will call to excuse the absence.

note:
Grades run from 1 to 5:
• о̏дличан - 5
• вр̏ло до̏бар - 4
• до̏бар - 3
• до̏во̄љан - 2
• не̏дово̄љан - 1

A two is a pass and a one is a fail, hence the teacher's «Седи, један!».

More school phrases:
• «Загреј ту столицу!» - sit there until you have learned it
• «Понављање је мајка знања» - repetition is the mother of learning
• «Зваће мама да оправда» - Mom will call to excuse the absence
title: Grades and school phrases

skip: a comparison of Serbian and Russian schools

note:
An address goes: street, house number, у̀лаз (entrance), спра̏т (floor), ста̑н (apartment).

In a long building each entrance has its own house number: entrance 3 - number 35, entrance 2 - number 34.

Floors are counted from zero: при́зе̄мље is 0, so an American 5th floor is a Serbian 4th.

The door code is ши̏фра, the intercom is и̏нтерфон. In a code «*» is called звѐздица and «#» is тараба.
title: Address and floors

note:
Uncles and aunts:
• стри̑ц and стри̑на - the father's brother and his wife
• у̏ја̄к and у̏јна - the mother's brother and his wife
• те̏тка and те̏ча - a parent's sister and her husband

Nephews and nieces:
• не̏ћа̄к and не̏ћака - the general words
• се̏стрић and сестрѝчина - a sister's children
• сино̀вац and синовица - a brother's children

The husband's relatives: свѐкар, све̏крва, де̏вер, за̏ова, јѐтрва.

The wife's relatives: та̏ст, та̏шта, шу̏рак.

In practice Serbs just say «бра̏т од те́тке» or simply «брат».
title: Relatives: стриц, ујак, теча and the rest

related.en: hot rakija with sugar and spices

note:
The main drink is ра̀кија, a fruit brandy made from plums (шљи̏вовица), apricots, pears and quinces.

Red wine is called «црно» (black), white wine «бело».

Cocktails:
• ба̀мбус - red wine with cola, a favorite of young people
• шпри̏цер - white wine with mineral water, for older people

In winter people drink «кувано вино» (mulled wine) and «кувану ракију» with sugar and spices.

Liqueurs: медо̀вача, орахова̀ча, вишњѐвача. Бѐрмет is wine with herbs.
title: What Serbs drink

note:
What is sold where:
• пи̏љарница - fruit and vegetables
• посластѝчарница - cakes and pastries
• пржионица кафе - coffee roasted on the spot
• мѐња̄чница - currency exchange
• чарапа̀ра - socks and underwear
• позаментерија - thread and sewing supplies
• кантѝна - a snack bar at a school or workplace

Бу̀тик is any small shop, the same as ду̀ћа̄н. A кинеска радња sells almost everything, and an апотека sells cosmetics and toys as well as medicines.
title: Names of shops

related.en: Nole, professor! (a fan chant about Novak Djokovic)
rip it up, go for it

note:
Addressing a man as «Професоре!» expresses approval and admiration, especially among men. People also say «ма̑јсторе», «легендо», «ца̏ре».

Fans sing «Ноле, професоре!» to Novak Djokovic.

Slang that comes from there:
• «гази!» - step on it, push forward
• «цепај!» - rip it up
title: The vocative as a compliment

note:
Key words of the Serbian character:
• пола́ко - not just «slowly» but a way of life without hurry
• ѝна̄т - stubbornness for the sake of stubbornness, part of the Serbs' self-image; an angry person switches on ѝна̄т and will not give an inch
• «ма̏ло су̏тра» - «not a chance»
• a red thread on the wrist (црвени конац) guards against the evil eye, especially children and pregnant women

Children in Serbia are «little gods».
title: Key words of the Serbian character

note:
Many words of everyday life and cooking came from Turkish:
• food: ра̀кија, а̀јва̄р, ка̀јмак, ће̏вап, ћу̀фте, су̏тлија̄ш
• everyday life and character: ду̀ћа̄н, ѝна̄т
• џа̏нум - «my dear» (literally «my soul»), heard in a song by Tea Dora

If you know Turkish, these words are easy to recognize, and the other way round.
title: Turkisms on the Serbian table

related.en: family feast of the patron saint

note:
Serbia's entries on UNESCO's list of intangible heritage:
• сла̏ва - the yearly feast of a family's patron saint
• ко̏ло - a round dance
• пе̏ва̄ње уз гу̏сле - epic poetry sung to a bowed instrument
• злакуска лончарија - pottery
• ра̀кија шљи̏вовица (since late 2022)

Крсна слава passes from father to son. In the song «Тамо далеко» the hero loses his home and «моју крсну славу».
title: Slava and UNESCO heritage
